facts.fact_text: On 2 March 2008 at around 12.30 p.m. the applicant arrived at Theatre Square in central Gyumri.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant tried to enter Theatre Square in central Gyumri in order to hold a protest.
It is alleged that the applicant started calling on people who were present at Theatre Square to gather and to hold a demonstration.
On 2 March 2008 the applicant was refused entry to Theatre Square by police officers who were stationed there for the purpose of preventing any demonstrations from taking place.
Police officers ordered the applicant to leave Theatre Square and to stop inciting others to assemble.
The applicant was taken to a police station after disobeying the police officers' orders at Theatre Square on 2 March 2008.
The Administrative Court made reference to Sections 2, 12, 22 and 38 of the Police Act (2001).

The Administrative Court held that mass public events may be held only after notification in writing to the competent authority, in this case the Head of the Gyumri Community, in accordance with the requirements of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as in force at the material time, provided that disobeying a lawful order of a military serviceman or a police officer issued in the performance of his duties of preserving public order and of ensuring public safety would result in a fine in the amount of 50 times the fixed minimum wage.
Section 38 of the Police Act (2001) provides that every citizen and public official is obliged to obey lawful orders of a police officer.

Section 38 of the Police Act (2001) provides that failure to obey lawful orders of a police officer or actions obstructing the performance of a police officer's duties result in liability in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.

The Administrative Court found that the conduct of a mass public event in Gyumri, the second largest city of the country, could have endangered the protection of public order and public health, particularly when no notification to hold such an event had been submitted in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

The Decree of the President of the Republic of Armenia No. NH-35-N declared a state of emergency in Yerevan from 1 March 2008 for 20 days, in order to prevent the threat of danger to the constitutional order in the Republic of Armenia and to protect the rights and lawful interests of the population, guided by point 14 of Article 55 and point 6 of Article 117 of the Constitution of the Republic of Armenia.

The Decree of the President of the Republic of Armenia No. NH-35-N established as a temporary limitation in the area under state of emergency the banning of meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches and other mass events.
The rallies on 1 March 2008 involved clashes between some protesters and law enforcement officers.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in ten deaths, including eight civilians.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in numerous injured persons.
The events of 1 March 2008 resulted in destruction of private and public property.

The police asserted that well-known facts included the fact that a tense situation had been created in Armenia after the tragic events of 1 March 2008, which threatened national security and public safety.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Ad-Hoc Public Report found that though the state of emergency was declared only in the City of Yerevan, some restrictions specified in the Decree declaring a state of emergency were effectively applied in other towns of Armenia as well, including the restriction of the freedom of assembly.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Report on the Functioning of Democratic Institutions in Armenia (Doc. 11579, 15 April 2008), produced by the co-rapporteurs of the PACE Committee on the Honouring of Obligations and Commitments by Member States of the Council of Europe (the Monitoring Committee), stated that although the state of emergency was formally only declared in Yerevan, a large number of provisions, especially those related to the media and the activities of political parties and NGOs, had a nationwide application.

The Report by the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights on his Special Mission to Armenia on 12-15 March 2008 (CommDH(2008)11REV, 20 March 2008) stated that a number of restrictions enacted by the state of emergency affected the whole country and were not limited to the boundaries of the capital.
